one_liner: Binary trace/telemetry logger with deferred formatting; its call-site enqueue beats vsprintf-to-buffer and printf-to-console in its own test.
what_it_does: P7 is a C++ library (with C, C# and Python wrappers) that records trace messages and numeric telemetry samples from an application and ships them through a pluggable sink: UDP to the Baical server, a binary file, a text file, console, syslog, Auto or Null. You create an IP7_Client from an option string ("/P7.Sink=FileBin /P7.Pool=4096", also overridable from the command line) and IP7_Trace or IP7_Telemetry channels on it, then log with printf-style macros such as P7_TRACE/P7_QTRACE. It is not a drop-in for printf or iostream: binary output is read with the Baical viewer/server, and text output goes through the slower text sinks.
how_it_is_fast: Deferred formatting with binary records: each call site's format string, file, function, line and module are serialized once as a 'description' (looked up by a fixed trace ID in an array, or by an RB-tree keyed on function and format-string addresses), and every later call writes only a small header (level, CPU, thread ID, sequence, 100 ns timestamp) plus the raw va_arg values, whose types were parsed from the format string once. Records are copied into a preallocated buffer pool and written or sent by a background thread, so the caller never formats or does I/O. The hot path is not lock-free: it takes a per-channel recursive pthread mutex and then the sink's mutex.
when_to_use: High-volume diagnostic tracing (hundreds of thousands to millions of messages per second from C/C++) where you can read logs in a dedicated viewer instead of grep.
You want trace plus numeric telemetry counters (CPU, queue depth, latencies) in one tool, with live streaming to a Baical server on another machine and remote verbosity control.
Mixed-language processes (C, C++, C#, Python) that should log into one trace stream, or channels shared across modules by name via shared memory.
Crash-time capture matters: P7_Set_Crash_Handler() installs a handler for segfaults, division by zero and similar faults that calls P7_Exceptional_Flush to save or send buffered records.
when_not_to_use: You need plain-text logs as the primary output: the manual's own sink ranking puts text file at about 0.9M/s, syslog 0.5M/s and console 0.1M/s, versus about 10M/s for the binary file sink, so most of the advantage disappears once P7 has to format text.
Many threads log to the same channel: every call serializes on two mutexes, unlike the per-thread lock-free queues in Quill, fmtlog or NanoLog.

You need a maintained dependency: this CMake port stopped at v5.2.0 in February 2020 (issue #4 points to an upstream 5.3.0 that was never merged), and issues about Clang builds (#1), 'unknown type name size_t' (#7) and timestamps jumping back two days on CentOS 7 (#2) are open with no replies.
LGPL-3.0-or-later is a problem for static linking in closed-source products (the CMake default builds a static library).
Lossless delivery is required: when the buffer pool is full or the sink is not connected, Trace() returns FALSE and the message is dropped (counted in reject counters), not blocked.

integration.form: static lib (default) or shared lib via CMake (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the OS: pthread and rt on Linux, ws2_32 on Windows
integration.min_toolchain: CMake 3.10; C++ standard not documented (pre-C++11 style code); MSVC and GCC; Clang build reported failing in Visual Studio (issue #1)
integration.platforms: Linux x86/x64 and Windows x86/x64 per the manual; ARM atomics code and ARM 926EJ numbers exist but ARM is not in the supported list
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe per the manual; implemented with a recursive pthread mutex per channel plus a mutex in the sink, so concurrent writers to one channel serialize

gotchas: Harness flaw in Tests/Speed/Speed.cpp: the P7 loop ignores Trace()'s return value and the client's reject counters, and the test passes no sink, so the default sink is Baical over UDP; run without a reachable Baical server (or without /P7.Sink=File on the command line) every call returns FALSE right after the mutex because the channel is not 'connected', and the dropped calls are reported as P7 throughput.

The same test sets /P7.Pool=65536 (64 MB, 16x the 4 MB default), so all 100,000 records fit in memory and the timed loop never meets back-pressure from the writer thread; the timer also stops before Release(), so file or network delivery is never timed.

Speed.cpp measures whole milliseconds: at about 5M calls/s the 100,000-call P7 loop takes about 19-20 ms, so the printed rate moves in 5% steps (100,000/19 ms = 5.26M, /20 ms = 5.00M); the manual's 5,210,000/s figure matches neither, which fits the verifier's finding that the screenshot came from a different build of the test.

The baselines are not like for like: the buffer case runs vsprintf with 6 arguments including two strings, the P7 case stores 1 integer and defers formatting, and the console case calls printf with the previous formatted line as its format string.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick P7 over binlog or Quill when you want the Baical tooling: live network streaming, telemetry graphs next to traces, remote verbosity control and C#/Python clients in the same stream. For a maintained, permissively licensed, multi-thread-scalable logger with text output, Quill or fmtlog are the better choices, and binlog is the closest maintained equivalent of P7's binary deferred-format design.
verified_claims_summary: The author's own speed test on an Intel i7-870 (2015, file sink, compiler and flags not stated) reports 5.21M P7 trace calls per second versus 688k vsprintf calls into a memory buffer and 10k printf calls to the console; the P7 number times only the enqueue into a 64 MB in-memory pool, not formatting or delivery, and no logging library was used as a baseline.
status_note: Abandoned port (last commit 2020-02-06, v5.2.0, upstream 5.3.0 never merged, six open issues without replies) but self-contained, dependency-free and copyable under LGPL-3.0-or-later; treat the speed figures as first-party and the benchmark as a best-case enqueue measurement.
